topic: Research: Coasty: An API for Computer-Use Agents

key_points: Official API reference: 'The Coasty Computer Use API gives your code the ability to see a screen and act on it.' You send a screenshot + plain-language instruction, the model returns typed actions (clicks, keystrokes, scrolls, drags) with pixel coordinates; your program executes them and loops.

Pure REST at https://coasty.ai/v1 — no SDK, no websocket required for core endpoints, stateless unless you opt into a session. Auth via X-API-Key (canonical) or Authorization: Bearer; pasting literal 'Bearer' inside X-API-Key is the most common first-day 401 INVALID_API_KEY.

Layered surface: /v1/predict (stateless workhorse), /v1/sessions (stateful screenshot loop), /v1/runs (agent drives a task on a machine to completion), /v1/tasks (submit-and-forget: provision + run + verify + cleanup), /v1/workflows (branching/looping multi-step automations), /v1/machines (managed cloud VMs), /v1/schedules (cron/webhook/email triggers), /v1/ground (x,y coordinates), /v1/parse (free deterministic pyautogui-to-action parsing).
Sandbox keys (sk-coasty-test-*) never bill and run against mock VMs (<50ms) with the same request/response shapes, so CI can run before flipping to a live key.

BYOK (PUT /v1/llm/keys/{provider}): the entire harness — worker, grounding, code agent, compaction — runs on your own Anthropic/OpenAI account; LLM steps bill $0 Coasty credits but your provider charges your key directly and machine runtime stays billable.

Marketing/product page: '#1 Computer-Use AI Agent | 82% OSWorld Benchmark', 'One call. Four lines. Built for any stack.', screenshot-in/actions-out with 'No selectors. No DOM parsing. No brittle XPath. Just vision.'

Machines API framed as 'Real desktops. Real shells. Real automation.' — 15 endpoints covering provision, start/stop/snapshot, screenshot, connection, actions (single + batch), browser ops, terminal, files.

Schedules API: cron, HMAC webhooks, email triggers, chains; per-fire limits (10 cr/min, webhook routing 1 cr per 200 fires, sandbox free). Schedules created via API appear in the dashboard automatically.
Explicitly positioned as built for any stack with no SDK lock-in and no browser drivers.
Third-party hands-on/setup writeup: describes Coasty as a YC S26 computer-use agent API that controls desktop and web apps via screenshots, mouse and keyboard 'no DOM access or selectors needed'.
Published API v1.0.0 surfaces: /v1/predict, /v1/triggers/webhook/{webhook_id} (no auth), managed VM provisioning, scheduled automation.

Cites $0.05 per /v1/predict, 1,000+ native app integrations (Gmail, Slack, Salesforce, HubSpot, Linear, GitHub, Stripe), free sandbox keys, public OpenAPI 3.1 spec at coasty.ai/openapi.json, and a $99 flat Unlimited dashboard plan.
Step 3 recommends the MCP server (https://api.coasty.ai/mcp) for Claude/Cursor integration — signals that MCP is the intended path for coding agents.

Independent review, 7.5/10, published 2026-07-09: 'The most credible RPA replacement of the year, with self-healing vision automation and a real free tier. The credit system just needs clearer explanation.'
Strongest use case is legacy software with no API — insurance portals, mainframes, 20-year-old desktop apps — where vision beats connectors and selectors.
Praises human-in-the-loop approval gates on high-stakes steps and a full audit trail (screenshot behind every action) for regulated work like healthcare billing.

Key caveats: the pricing page never explains what counts as a credit; 82% accuracy is best-in-class but mistakes still happen; 'skip Coasty if your systems already have clean APIs' because code will be cheaper and more reliable.

Vendor comparison that maps the alternative landscape the article must position against: Browser Use (autonomous Python agents, re-reasons every step, DOM-first), Stagehand (TypeScript AI methods layered on Playwright, caches actions to cut repeat-run cost), Skyvern (single API, computer vision, Planner-Actor-Validator, cross-site generalization).

Browser Use and Stagehand are libraries you maintain and pay per LLM call; Skyvern/Coasty sell a hosted API where the loop, retries and selectors are not your problem — the core 'framework vs API' split.
Independent computer-use leaderboard (updated March 2026) covering OSWorld, OSWorld-Verified and ScreenSpot-Pro.
On independently assessed OSWorld the top entries are Claude Opus 4.6 at 72.7% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 72.5%, with human baseline 72.4% — Coasty does not appear in the independently evaluated table.

GPT-5.4's 75.0% is on OSWorld-Verified and self-reported; the page explicitly separates 'assessed by the research team' from 'self-reported by provider' — the exact distinction a skeptical review of Coasty's 82–85.6% claim must make.

Coasty's own benchmark blog: claims 82% on OSWorld vs OpenAI Operator 38/38.1%, Anthropic Computer Use 22%, UiPath Screen Agent (Claude Opus 4.5) 72%; argues the gap is architecture (real desktops/browsers/terminals, not API calls).

This is vendor-published marketing for the exact number the review must audit — it mixes 'Anthropic Computer Use agent scored 22%' (the 2024 launch score) with current Claude model scores, which is the main rhetorical sleight of hand.

Anthropic's own docs frame computer use as a model-level TOOL ('Give Claude screenshot, mouse, and keyboard control'), not a managed service: you supply the loop, the machine, the execution and the storage.

Billing is per token (input screenshots + system prompt + tool definitions) with no managed-VM, run-record or audit layer — which is exactly the operational layer Coasty sells; the Coasty review's 'harness vs model' angle should cite this page as the baseline.
Fetched 2026-10-01 via curl (HTTP 200); the docs index lists 'Computer use tool' alongside a separate 'Browser use tool', i.e. the primitives Coasty wraps are documented but unhosted.

OpenAI documents computer use as an API tool inside its Tools surface (same pattern as Anthropic): the model returns actions, your application runs them; availability/limits change independently of any vendor benchmark snapshot.
No managed desktops, no per-step price card, no workflow/schedule/HITL surface is published on this page — useful contrast for the review's 'raw model vs hosted CUA API' section.
Fetched 2026-10-01 via curl (HTTP 200); page is a JS-heavy docs shell, so use the .md variant of a page URL (the docs advertise appending .md) when quoting exact text.

stats.fact: Coasty reports 85.6% on OSWorld from its in-house model (results/traces public at github.com/coasty-ai/coasty-osworld) and 82.81% from its public model on the official OSWorld leaderboard; the same source lists OpenAI Operator at 38.1%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 72.5% and the human baseline at 72.4%.

Independent OSWorld leaderboard (March 2026) top entries: Claude Opus 4.6 72.7%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.5%, Qwen3 VL 235B 66.7%; human baseline 72.4%. Coasty is not listed among independently evaluated entries.

OSWorld-Verified (as of Sep 2026) is led by self-reported scores (Qwen3.8-Max 86.1%, Claude Mythos Preview 85.4%); the tracker labels these 'self-reported by Alibaba/Anthropic', not independently verified.

On the harder OSWorld 2.0 (108 long-horizon tasks, median ~1.6 human hours each, revised July 2026), the best agent reaches only 20.6% binary completion and needs ~318 tool calls per task (~10.6x the old benchmark) — the headline 85% on OSWorld-Verified does not transfer to realistic long-horizon work.

Subscription pricing: Starter $19/mo (200 credits, 1 machine, 3 swarm agents, 3 schedules), Plus $50/mo (600 credits, 2 machines, 6 agents, 10 schedules), Unlimited $99/mo (unlimited credits, 2 machines, 5 agents, 10 schedules). Boost packs: 150 cr/$19, 500 cr/$49, 1,200 cr/$99 (require a paid subscription).

Metered API rates (1 credit = $0.01): POST /v1/predict 5 credits ($0.05 base, surcharges can apply); POST /v1/sessions 10 credits fixed to open + 4 credits ($0.04) per stateful predict step; POST /v1/ground 3 credits ($0.03); POST /v1/parse free (0 credits, deterministic; no LLM cost).

Documented predict surcharges: +2 credits per provider-visible prior trajectory screenshot, +1 credit per HD current/trajectory image larger than 1280x720, +3 credits on the v1 engine (v3/v4/v5 add 0), and +1 credit when system_prompt + instructions exceeds 500 characters. Real cost is therefore workload- and history-dependent, not a flat $0.05.

Agent-run billing: managed runs default to $0.05 (5 credits) per completed agent step with the current engine, vs $0.08/step on the legacy v1 engine; BYOK runs bill $0 Coasty credits for LLM steps and machine runtime remains the only Coasty charge.

Public contract size: OpenAPI 3.1 spec with 65 paths and 81 operations across Predict, Sessions, Ground, Parse, Machines, Schedules, Runs, Tasks, Workflows, Keys, Billing and Usage; sandbox keys mock a VM in under 50ms and bill 0 credits.
stats.source: https://coasty.ai/openapi.json (fetched and counted directly) and https://coasty.ai/llms.txt

stats.fact: Integrations: 1,000+ OAuth-secured apps and 20,000+ individual tools via Composio, callable inside any task; when an app has an API Coasty calls it directly, when it does not the agent drives the UI. Named examples include Salesforce, HubSpot, Slack, Gmail, Notion, Linear, Jira, GitHub, Stripe, Shopify.
First-party MCP server exposes 26 tools (predict, machines, schedules, account, discovery groups) and works in Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf and VS Code Copilot Agent.

Task runs require runs:read/runs:write and support a hard max_steps (default 150, ceiling 1,000), deadline_seconds, action_policy (cumulative max_actions inherited by nested delegation) and on_awaiting_human (pause/fail/cancel). POST /v1/tasks deliberately makes human takeover impossible — it suppresses awaiting_human and treats CAPTCHAs/email confirmations as part of the task.

Security model: a key minted without an explicit scopes array gets 20 default scopes; exactly three are opt-in privilege escalations — connection:read (returns plaintext SSH keys/VNC passwords), browser:execute (arbitrary JS in the VM browser) and keys (mints new API keys). A key can never mint a key with scopes it does not hold.

Governance/verification gap: independent API-readiness scoring gives Coasty a 'Contract Governance' facet of 4.5/100 (Discoverability 75.9, Contract Quality 67.2, Access Clarity 76.3; overall Kin Score 59.6/100), i.e. a good spec but weak deprecation/versioning governance.

Context for browser-only rivals: browser-use scores 89.1% on WebVoyager (586 live web tasks), Stagehand's agent primitive ~75% in third-party comparisons — so on pure web tasks the open-source frameworks are competitive with a general computer-use API.
Independent review score: 7.5/10 (MakerStack, July 2026) with a free tier that requires no credit card.

HN launch provenance: 'Launch HN: Coasty (YC S26) – An API for computer-use agents' was posted 2026-07-15 and drew 44 points / 26 comments — modest traction versus earlier CUA launches (Cua, YC X25, 172 points). Founder answers in-thread are the most concrete public evidence for two review claims: workflows pause at `awaiting_human` before irreversible steps (form submit, message send, payment confirm), and verification is framed around outcomes (confirmation page, reopening the submitted record, matching a reference ID) because 'a UI saying success is weak evidence'.
stats.source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48922706 (HN item 48922706, fetched via HN Algolia API 2026-10-01; 44 pts, 26 comments, posted 2026-07-15T15:51:20Z)

stats.fact: Compliance claim is founder-stated, not documented: in the same launch thread the founder asserts the company is 'SOC2 and HIPAA compliant' with zero-data-retention via an enterprise platform. The public developer docs carry the retention/encryption mechanics (AES-256-GCM screenshot storage decisions, account-lifetime audit rows) but no SOC2 report or HIPAA BAA link, so the review should attribute the certification to the founder's comment, not to published compliance artifacts.

GitHub footprint is thin relative to the marketing: the coasty-ai org (gh api orgs/coasty-ai/repos, 2026-10-01) lists coasty-osworld (4 stars, results/traces for OSWorld, last pushed 2026-06-28), llmhub-api (3), computer-use-cookbook (7), and open-cowork (144 stars, an unrelated open-source Claude Co-Work alternative, updated 2026-09-14). The vendor llms.txt describes an 'open-source framework' pointing at an Anthropic-namespaced repo; the public artifacts are actually per-domain OSWorld result dumps (chrome, gimp, libreoffice_*, multi_apps, os, thunderbird, vlc, vs_code) — there is no open-source server for the /v1 API.
stats.source: gh api orgs/coasty-ai/repos + repos/coasty-ai/coasty-osworld (2026-10-01), README of coasty-ai/coasty-osworld

stats.fact: The vendor's own 'independently verified' leaderboard URL is not machine-verifiable by fetch: https://osworld-v1.xlang.ai/ serves the OSWorld paper page, a raw fetch on 2026-10-01 contained zero occurrences of 'Coasty' (or '82.81'), and its 'OSWorld-Verified Results' block renders client-side ('Loading verified benchmark data...'). A reviewer can therefore only confirm Coasty's public trace repository, not the 82.81% on that page.
stats.source: direct curl of https://osworld-v1.xlang.ai/ (HTTP 200, 153 KB) on 2026-10-01; grep for 'Coasty'/'82.81' = 0 matches

stats.fact: Runtime cost comparators for the 'you still pay for the machine' caveat: E2B's published pricing is Hobby free ($100 one-time usage credit, 20 concurrent sandboxes), Pro $150/mo + per-second usage, Enterprise from $3,000/mo; Browserbase lists Free $0 (3 concurrent browsers, 1 browser hour), Developer $20/mo (25 concurrent, 100 browser hours then $0.12/browser-hr), Startup $99/mo (100 concurrent, 500 browser hours then $0.10/browser-hr). Coasty's managed machines are $0.05/hr Linux and $0.09/hr Windows running, $0.01/hr stopped, so VM time is cheap next to the per-step model charges.
stats.source: https://e2b.dev/pricing and https://www.browserbase.com/pricing and https://coasty.ai/llms.txt (all fetched 2026-10-01)

angles: The central tension: an 'API' review that must audit the marketing number, not repeat it. Coasty's 82–85.6% OSWorld figure is vendor-published (in-house model + self-submitted public model), while independently evaluated leaderboards list Claude Opus 4.6 at 72.7% and never list Coasty — the honest framing is 'best-in-class on OSWorld-Verified as self-reported, unlisted on independent eval'.

Why OSWorld-Verified is the wrong test anyway: OSWorld 2.0's long-horizon tasks drop the same frontier models to ~20.6% completion at ~10.6x the tool calls. A computer-use API sold as '85% reliable' should be procured against your own long-horizon workflow, not a 369-task micro-task suite.

The API-first argument that actually holds: Coasty sells the harness — managed VMs, screenshot loop, action executor, billing isolation, recovery, schedules, webhooks — not the model. Anthropic/OpenAI/Google give you a model that can click; they leave you to build the loop, retries, VM lifecycle and audit trail. That is the real differentiator, not the benchmark.

Cost transparency is the buyer's trap: $0.05/predict is a base fee, and surcharges (prior trajectory screenshots, HD images, >500-char prompts, legacy v1 engine) plus $0.04/stateful step and $0.05/completed agent step make real spend workload-dependent. The $99 'Unlimited' plan governs the consumer credit balance, not the developer API wallet — conflating them is the most likely pricing misunderstanding.

Framework vs API is the actual decision axis: Browser Use (MIT, Python, DOM-first, 89.1% WebVoyager) and Stagehand (TypeScript on Playwright, cached replays) are free libraries where you own the loop and pay only LLM tokens; Coasty/Skyvern sell the operational reliability layer. Choose the library if you have engineers, the API if you have workflows.

Lock-in is lower than it looks on the protocol layer (plain REST, OpenAPI 3.1, BYOK for the whole harness) and higher on the value layer (1,000+ Composio integrations, audit trails, schedules) — you can port your code but not the integration catalog or the compliance trail.

Security posture is a selling point with real teeth: per-session VM isolation, deny-by-default typed actions (action_type+params authoritative, raw_code never executed), HITL approval gates, no CAPTCHA-solver or proxy-evasion claims — but three opt-in scopes (connection:read, browser:execute, keys) are genuine privilege escalations that CI keys should never hold.

'Skip it if you have clean APIs' — the vendor's own reviewers concede the honest boundary: vision-based UI control wins on legacy/desktop/no-API software (insurance portals, mainframes, internal tools) and loses on anything with an endpoint.

The launch thread is the review's most useful primary source and the least used: the founder's own answers concede that screenshot-after-action verification fails when 'the UI is lying about form state' (a React controlled select renders the right value while the framework state never commits) and that they counter it with outcome checks and human gates — an unusually candid statement of the category's core limitation, straight from the vendor.

Price the *whole* deployment, not the predict call: $0.05/predict is the visible number, but a run at 150 steps ≈ $7.50 in model charges on top of $0.05/hr Linux machines and $0.01/snapshot — cheap VM, expensive loop. That inversion is where a buyer's spreadsheet and Coasty's headline price diverge.
